headlines.title: San Jose firefighters battle vegetation fire near I-280 on-ramp
headlines.description: San Jose firefighters are responding to a vegetation fire burning near an Interstate 280 on-ramp. The San Jose Fire Department said crews are on the scene in the 0 block of Duane Street, near the I-280 on-ramp from South First Street. At last report, the fire had consumed approximately a half-acre. Fire officials stated that no structures are currently threatened. Authorities are urging the public to avoid the area while firefighters work to contain the blaze.

headlines.title: Preliminary 4.1 magnitude earthquake strikes Mendocino County
headlines.description: A preliminary 4.1 magnitude earthquake struck in Mendocino County, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 5:25 p.m. Tuesday and was centered in Covelo, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Pedestrian taken to hospital after being hit by driver in San Jose
headlines.description: A pedestrian was taken to a hospital with major injuries Tuesday after they were struck by a driver in San Jose, police said. The collision happened at about 12:05 p.m. in the area of Tully Road and Lucretia Avenue, according to police. The driver stayed at the scene and was cooperative with investigators, police said. Additional information wasn’t immediately available. An investigation is ongoing.

headlines.title: Dallas boy, 10, thanks California lifeguard who rescued him from powerful waves
headlines.description: Back home in Dallas, 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai is still dealing with the aftershock of nearly losing his life on a California beach last month. “I was pretty much on the shore, [and] I got like pulled,” Nathaniel told NBC 5. Nathaniel, who has now seen the viral video of himself being rescued, said he was on a family vacation when their beach day ended with him almost drowning. “I screamed for help,” he said. That call was answered by a 16-year-old lifeguard, Ryder Williams, who said he saw Nathaniel lose his footing. Williams radioed for help as he rushed into the water. “I think one more wave happened and I went unconscious,” Nathaniel said. “When I woke up, Ryder was taking me to shore … I was super thankful because I knew he was going to save my life.” Ryder has been called a hero for saving the boy’s life, but he said he was simply doing the job he loved. Only a few days ago, Nathaniel and his dad got to speak to him to express their gratitude. “I was like, ‘Thank you so much for saving my life and my sister thanked him,'” Nathaniel said. That thank you led to a video chat with both families, according to Nathaniel’s father, Sumit Rai. He said in a serendipitous way, they now feel connected. “It turns out there’s a lot of commonalities between us,” Rai said. “We all really like UFC, so we’re talking about going to a fight together … It also so happens that [Ryder’s father] is a retired firefighter and Ryder wants to follow in his footsteps and be a firefighter. I happen to run a nonprofit for firefighters to screen them for cancer.” It was a scary, tragic situation that revealed that some moments can reveal something bigger. Nathaniel and his dad said they are grateful for it all.

headlines.title: Back to school: Bay Area teachers spend their own money to get supplies they need
headlines.description: As Bay Area teachers prepare for the new school year, many are digging into their own pockets to buy supplies. In the South Bay, most teachers head to a nonprofit called RAFT. It’s a special spot in San Jose with 32,000 square feet of discounted classroom items. “Our educators come here because it’s very, very low cost,” RAFT’s Kate Ball said. “A lot of teachers are sometimes expected to pay out of pocket to supply their classrooms, so we’re trying to help that need.” RAFT said teachers spend between $500 and $1,000 per year on school supplies. At Santee Elementary School in San Jose on Tuesday, Imelda Murillo was getting her classroom ready for her students, who arrive on Monday. “Sometimes we do have donations, like tissue, Kleenex, and things like that, which doesn’t seem like a school would need, but we do,” she said. “Paper towels – sometimes we run out of paper towels – hand soap, disinfectant wipes, those kinds of things that you don’t necessarily think are related to an education, but we need all of those things.” Teachers are given a stipend for the school year. District officials said they wish they could give more. At campuses like Santee, teachers said it’s not nearly enough to cover the costs of giving children the quality education they deserve.

headlines.title: Air quality advisory issued as wildfire smoke drifts into the Bay Area
headlines.description: The Bay Area Air District issued an air quality advisory for Tuesday and Wednesday as wildfire smoke from the Pacific Northwest is expected to drift into the region. While the district said pollution levels are not expected to exceed the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s 24-hour health standard for fine particulate matter — which measures the average concentration of pollution over the course of a day — air quality could still become unhealthy at times as smoke conditions shift. According to the district, residents might notice smoky skies, haze and the smell of smoke, but changing weather patterns make it tough to predict where smoke will settle at ground level. Wildfire smoke holds fine particulate matter and other pollutants that can irritate the eyes and airways, cause coughing and worsen respiratory conditions like asthma, emphysema and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Older adults, children and people with respiratory illnesses are especially vulnerable to smoke exposure. Air Quality Aug 19, 2021 Foster City Aug 3 bay area weather 10 hours ago To reduce health risks, the district recommends that people stay inside with the windows and doors closed. If smoke becomes significant, setting air conditioning systems to recirculate or seeking buildings with filtered air, such as libraries or shopping malls, would be best. The Bay Area Air District said it will continue to monitor air quality throughout the region, and encouraged residents to check the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Fire and Smoke Map for real-time air quality conditions in their area at fire.airnow.gov.

headlines.title: Shelter-in-place lifted after Novato shooting leaves 1 injured
headlines.description: One person suffered life-threatening injuries in a shooting in Novato on Tuesday morning that prompted authorities to tell nearby residents to shelter in place, police said. Officers responded at about 10:10 a.m. to the 400 block of Alameda del Prado, where callers reported hearing multiple shots fired and then a suspect running away from the area, according to Novato police. A male victim was found with a life-threatening gunshot wound and was taken to a hospital, police said. Investigators believe the victim and suspect knew each other. Police are still searching for the suspect, who is described as a Hispanic man standing about 5 feet, 6 inches tall with dark pants and a gray hooded sweatshirt, and wearing a black mask. He was last seen fleeing toward Calle Arboleda. People on Alameda del Prado and Calle Arboleda were initially told to shelter in place following the shooting. Novato police later lifted the shelter-in-place order and reopened Alameda del Prado between Ignacio Boulevard and Posada del Sol. Police said the Marin County Sheriff’s Office and California Highway Patrol assisted with the search, along with a canine team from the Vallejo Police Department. Anyone with information about the suspect’s whereabouts is asked to call 911. Anyone with other information related to the case should call 415-897-4361 or email crimetips@novato.gov. Tipsters can remain anonymous.

headlines.title: Suspected DUI driver arrested after deadly crash on Highway 17 in Campbell
headlines.description: A 21-year-old Los Gatos man suspected of driving under the influence of alcohol was arrested early Tuesday following a fiery crash on Highway 17 in Campbell that left another driver dead, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision happened at about 2:48 a.m. on southbound Highway 17, just north of Hamilton Avenue, the CHP said. The Los Gatos man was behind the wheel of a Dodge Challenger when he crashed into the back of a Toyota Tacoma, causing that driver to lose control, the CHP said, citing a preliminary investigation. The Tacoma then became fully engulfed in flames, according to the CHP. The driver, a 47-year-old Campbell man, died at the scene. His identity wasn’t immediately known. The Los Gatos man was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and causing death or serious bodily injury, the CHP said. Authorities did not immediately release his identity. The crash remains under investigation, the CHP said. Anyone who witnessed it or has information about it is asked to contact the CHP San Jose Area Office at 408-961-0900.

headlines.title: National Night Out brings neighbors, first responders together across Bay Area
headlines.description: Communities across the Bay Area will celebrate National Night Out on Tuesday, the annual event that brings neighbors and first responders together to strengthen community ties. The San Mateo Police Department is among dozens of law enforcement agencies participating in this year’s event. National Night Out gives families an opportunity to meet police officers, firefighters and other first responders who serve their communities outside of emergency situations. The events are designed to provide a fun, family-friendly setting where residents can get to know the people who help keep their neighborhoods safe. NBC Bay Area’s Ali Reid has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by alleged DUI driver in hit and run in San Jose
headlines.description: San Jose police on Sunday arrested a suspected drunken driver who allegedly struck and killed a pedestrian before fleeing the scene. The collision happened at about 2:16 a.m. Sunday in the area of Bernal Road and Via Del Oro in South San Jose, according to police. Citing a preliminary investigation, police said a man behind the wheel of a Chevrolet pickup truck was heading eastbound on Bernal Road when he hit a pedestrian who was on Bernal Road at its intersection with Via Del Oro. The pedestrian, a man, succumbed to his injuries and died at the scene, police said. His identity will be released by the medical examiner’s office. The driver fled from the scene of the collision before officers arrived, police said, but officers later found him. He was determined to be under the influence of alcohol, arrested, and booked into jail for driving under the influence, vehicular manslaughter, and felony hit and run. This marked San Jose’s 26th deadly traffic collision and 12th pedestrian death of 2026, according to police. An investigation is ongoing.

headlines.title: California implements new regulations on generative AI
headlines.description: A landmark state law requiring notification about content created by generative artificial intelligence went into effect over the weekend, creating a new regulatory framework in California that will soon also apply to social media content and recording devices. The state’s Sunday implementation date was timed to coincide with regulators in the European Union, in what the legislation’s co-author, State Sen. Josh Becker, D-Menlo Park, said was unprecedented coordination between the two governments. The California AI Transparency Act requires companies that use generative artificial intelligence — which is sometimes referred to as GenAI or gen AI — to provide digital evidence that discloses that fact to a consumer in the metadata like a digital signature or fingerprint. Or, as Becker called it during a news conference from the state Capitol in Sacramento on Monday, a “nutrition list” of what ingredients went into making the content. Becker elaborated on the new law and a new bill that could modify the portion of the law that restricts its application to products that have over 1 million users. The new bill, Senate Bill 1000, would make the regulation apply to any generative AI product, regardless of the size of its userbase. The bill would also clarify that the onus is on content creation tools to include the digital information to be in compliance. Becker said the law will help content consumers trust what they were seeing online, saying it was aimed at stopping deepfakes, scams, and creating uncertainty around elections. “This is the beginning of a foundational change on how content is represented on the internet,” Becker said. He said the legislation’s long runway giving companies time to comply was to ensure the requirements were “technically feasible — that the companies can implement it and will be expected to implement it and comply.” The law was first passed in 2024 and its implementation date was delayed in 2025 to August to both coordinate its activation with the European Union and gave artificial intelligence companies more time to implement technology that would make the companies own products that generate images, text, audio, or other content compliant with the law. Neither Meta nor Google responded to requests for comment Monday on whether they were complying as of the legislation’s deadline. The law also gives companies hosting social media users’ content until Jan. 1 to ensure that their sites are compliant, including user-generated content. The key provision that kicked in this week requires companies that offer generative AI to offer users a free tool that can disclose whether content was created with those tools by displaying information about how it was created, while keeping information from the creator private. Website owners must first verify that content appearing on the site carries common metadata about its creation, such as what tool or software was involved. The law states websites offering such content must offer a tool that clearly lets users verify the content’s “authenticity, origin, or history of modification, including, but not limited to, all of the following: whether provenance data is available, the name of the GenAI system or capture device that created or substantially altered the content, if applicable, and whether any digital signatures are available.” Violators could face fines of up to $5,000 for each violation, and charges could be brought by local district attorneys or the Attorney General’s Office. David Evan Harris, a policy expert with the California Initiative for Technology and Democracy, known as CITED, said that the transparency provided by the regulation would help the evolving artificial intelligence sector gain stability and even empower new tech companies to provide such verification tools. He also said the state was filling a vacuum left by the federal government. “While Washington is abdicating responsibility for this, California and the E.U. are stepping forward,” he said. Eddan Katz, head of policy and government affairs with the technology start-up Encypher, said at the press conference that the regulations were written to make sure that technology that creates content makes a record of what it is doing. Encypher and a growing number of companies can then use tools to verify the record is there, rather than trying to detect artificial intelligence in the content. “We’ve actually changed the paradigm in which to think about battling this problem,” Katz said. Becker also said California was leading the way on AI regulation, with Washington state passing a similar law and New York currently considering one. The state’s requirements on devices that capture images and can manipulate them with generative artificial intelligence kick in starting in 2028.

headlines.title: East Bay salon owner forced to close after arson fire
headlines.description: An East Bay business owner is being forced to close her flourishing hair salon after an arsonist set fire to the shop over the weekend, wiping out a lifelong dream in mere minutes. The beauty shop, which specializes in weaves, braids, and cuts, has been a favorite spot in downtown Antioch for the past six years. Today, the storefront is boarded up. “I’m completely and utterly heartbroken,” owner Lala Perry said after the fire broke out early Sunday morning. While firefighters were able to contain the blaze to the back of the business, the intense smoke and heat left everything inside unusable. “It melted the plastic drawer, my mop, bucket, the lights,” Perry said. Officials assessed the building and informed Perry of the extensive ruin. “They said the walls are gonna have to be stripped. The flooring is going to have to be stripped. They’re gonna have to repair the structural damage,” she said. Firefighters confirmed the fire was intentionally set. “He said with certainty that it was arson, and it was started from the outside of our back door,” Perry noted. Fire investigators are currently reviewing surveillance video from a nearby business that shows a person on a bicycle pedaling into the alley behind the shop. A few minutes later, the individual pedals out as flames start to flare up. Investigators say they cannot confirm at this time if the bicyclist is connected to the fire, but they believe he may have information that could help the investigation. “The moment he races out of the alley is 4:57 a.m.,” Perry said. “I get my first alarm notification at 4:56 a.m. right before he races out.” The fire has severely impacted the livelihoods of five stylists at the salon. “This is our livelihood. This is the only way we make our money,” stylist Trenae Payton said. “I don’t have another job. I don’t have a 401(k). This is how I feed my two sons, 3 and 5. This is it. … I love this hair. I love [what I do].” The sudden closure has also left loyal customers upset. “The fact that they’re not gonna be here and maybe not even downtown, that’s sad,” customer Jacqueline Williams said. For Perry, a single mother who put her heart and soul into building her business, it feels like her life’s dream has been taken. She has started a GoFundMe campaign to replace what was lost and to relocate elsewhere. Despite the devastation, Perry remains defiant. “They lit a fire in our shop. We’ve got a fire under our butts,” Perry said. “We’re ready to keep going. We’re not giving up in any way, shape or form.”
